title: Rack-integrated quantum dot-based source of single and entangled photons at telecom C-band
authors: Michal Vyvlecka, Raphael Joos, Benjamin Breiholz, Emma Marmasse, Anna Friederike Köhler, Ponraj Vijayan, Tobias Huber-Loyola, Sven Höfling, Michael Jetter, Simone Luca Portalupi, Peter Michler
abstract: For quantum light sources in everyday telecommunication networks, quantum science needs to be fully transformed into quantum technology. The first necessary step to move outside a well-controlled lab environment requires the use of quantum light sources operating in the technologically relevant telecom O- and C-band. This can be provided using epitaxial quantum dots as deterministic sources of quantum light. Particularly intriguing is that emitters operating at telecom wavelengths are rapidly catching up with their short wavelength counterparts in terms of performances. Here, we make a decisive step forward in the development of quantum communication networks: a state-of-the-art source of quantum light, a semiconductor quantum dot (QD), with record coincidence rate for entangled photon emission in the telecom C-band, is operated inside an optimized rack-based setup. This setup includes a tunable pulsed laser for the QD excitation (from quasi- to fully resonant excitation), all optics for the excitation filtering, and QD signal coupling into single-mode fibers. Overall, the setup allows for above $50\%$ transmission for both exciton and biexciton photons. These results show that quantum dots-based telecom light sources can now be transported and integrated into existing fiber infrastructures, an important step to demonstrate the feasibility of the upcoming quantum internet.
summary: The research presents the development and testing of a compact, transportable source using semiconductor quantum dots to generate single and entangled photons directly at telecom C-band wavelengths. By integrating complex optical components into a field-ready rack, the authors demonstrate a major step toward realizing practical quantum internet infrastructure for secure communication.
main_problem: The primary challenge is transitioning quantum light sources from controlled laboratory settings into practical, field-deployable systems for quantum communication networks.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a compact, transportable source capable of emitting single and polarization-entangled photons at the telecom C-band with high efficiency and record coincidence rates.
method: They utilized semiconductor Quantum Dots (QDs) embedded in an optimized, rack-based setup that integrates multiple excitation lasers and optical components for field operation.
model_or_system: The system uses InAs/GaAs quantum dots grown on a metamorphic buffer layer, engineered to emit at telecom wavelengths. The source can be excited via various schemes, including LA-phonon-assisted or two-photon excitation (TPE), allowing control over single and entangled photon generation.
key_observables: Second-order correlation function ($g^{(2)}(0)$) confirming single-photon nature; high coincidence rates ($\sim 201 	ext{ kcps}$); entanglement fidelity ($\ge 0.964$); and calculated Secure Key Rates (SKR).
important_parameters: Operation at telecom C-band wavelengths; achieving $>50\%$ transmission efficiency; maintaining low multi-photon probability ($g^{(2)}(0) \ll 1$).
main_assumptions: The setup assumes the ability to integrate multiple complex laser sources and remote control mechanisms into a portable unit for field use.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the physical layout of the transportable source (color-coded floors), spectral measurements confirming excitation suppression, and characterization plots showing correlation functions and density matrices for entangled pairs.
paper_structure: The paper details the development of a state-of-the-art, compact hardware platform. It presents experimental results validating single-photon purity ($g^{(2)}$) and high-fidelity entanglement generation at telecom wavelengths, culminating in demonstrations of long-distance quantum key distribution potential.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum optics as it provides a concrete, scalable hardware platform for generating entangled photons necessary for quantum networking protocols like QKD.
